prompt: Which device has been used to verify the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution of molecular speeds experimentally?

choices.text: A velocity selector of spinning wheels with holes
A mass spectrometer that sorts the ions by their mass
choices.why: A mass spectrometer sorts by mass, not by speed. The section describes a velocity selector: a series of spinning wheels with holes that only molecules of one speed can pass.

choices.text: A manometer that measures the pressure of the gas
choices.why: The pressure is an average over all speeds and cannot show their spread. A velocity selector picks out one speed at a time, so the molecules at each speed can be counted.

choices.text: A thermometer placed in a stream of the gas
choices.why: A thermometer reads a single temperature, not a spread of speeds. The velocity selector, a series of spinning wheels with holes, counts molecules speed by speed.

explanation: A velocity selector is essentially a series of spinning wheels, each with a hole, through which the effused gas is sent. Only molecules of one speed pass all the holes, so the number at each speed can be counted.

prompt: In a velocity selector, gas molecules are sent through a series of spinning wheels, each with a hole. Why do only molecules of one particular speed get through all of the holes?

choices.text: They reach each wheel just as its hole comes by
A magnetic field in the wheels deflects the others
choices.why: No magnetic field is involved, and the molecules are not charged. What matters is timing: a molecule must arrive at each wheel just as its hole lines up.

choices.text: The holes are too small for the heavier molecules
choices.why: The holes do not sort by size or mass. A molecule gets through only if its speed brings it to each wheel just when the hole is in place.

choices.text: Faster molecules knock the slower ones aside
choices.why: The molecules are not sorted by colliding with each other. A molecule passes all the holes only if its speed matches the rate at which the holes come around.

explanation: The holes in successive wheels are set so that a molecule must cross the gap between wheels in exactly the time the next hole takes to come into place. A molecule that is too fast or too slow hits a solid part of a wheel.

prompt: How does a velocity selector measure the whole distribution of molecular speeds, rather than a single speed?

choices.text: Molecules are counted at many different spin rates
The temperature of the gas is changed step by step
choices.why: Changing T changes the distribution itself. To map one distribution, the gas is kept the same and the wheels are spun at various rates, each picking out a different speed.

choices.text: Wheels with holes of different sizes are swapped in
choices.why: The hole size does not pick the speed; the spin rate does. So the wheels are spun at various rates, and the molecules passing at each rate are counted.

choices.text: All the molecules pass, and each one is timed
choices.why: At one spin rate only one speed gets through. Spinning the wheels at various rates selects different speeds, and the count at each rate gives the distribution.

explanation: Each spin rate lets through molecules of one speed. Counting the molecules that pass at many different rates gives the number of molecules at each speed, which is the speed distribution.

prompt: What did the counts from velocity-selector experiments show about the speeds of gas molecules?

choices.text: All the molecules move at the same speed
choices.why: Molecules pass at many different spin rates, so their speeds are widely spread. That spread matches the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution.

choices.text: Every speed up to a maximum is equally common
choices.why: The counts are not flat: few molecules are very slow or very fast, and most are in between. This is the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution.

choices.text: Most molecules are at rest, with a few fast ones
choices.why: Very few molecules are nearly at rest. The counts peak at an intermediate speed, just as the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution predicts.

explanation: Counting molecules at various speeds showed that they do satisfy the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution. This is the experimental check on the distribution derived from kinetic theory.

prompt: In a velocity selector, two spinning wheels on the same axle are 0.40 m apart. The hole in the second wheel comes into line 0.80 ms after a molecule passes the hole in the first wheel. Only molecules that cover the 0.40 m in that time get through, so v = L/t. What speed do they have, in m/s?
explanation: v = L/t = (0.40 m)/(0.80 × 10^−3 s) = 500 m/s. Spinning the wheels faster shortens the delay and selects faster molecules.
